title: “Oops, did we include you?” Rethinking PBS through co-production with Steven
abstract: Purpose This paper aims to share the story of a co-produced functional behaviour assessment (FBA) with Steven, a young man who helped us rethink what it really means to involve someone in their own support. Using observation, data collection and analysis, the authors made the process accessible and collaborative by working alongside Steven to ensure it was meaningful and person-led. Design/methodology/approach With shared activities, humour and trust, Steven did not just contribute to his plan; he shaped it. Findings In response to concerns about assumption-driven planning and tokenistic involvement in positive behaviour support (Gore et al., 2022), the authors reimagined the FBA with Steven as a co-designer, guided by functional contextualism to ensure meaning was derived from his perspective (McGill, 1996). His insights changed how we thought about behaviour, communication and what good support looks like. Originality/value This is not a how-to guide. It is a reflection on what changes when we centre the person from the beginning, and why co-production is essential.

title: Will consumers continue to use smart wearable devices? Validating the technology integration model
journal: Asia Pacific Journal of Marketing and Logistics
abstract: Purpose Despite numerous studies investigating continuance intention to use smart wearable devices (SWDs), an understanding of the integration of technology features and human psychological factors in a single model is limited. This study aims to examine factors that influence the continuance intention to use SWDs by empirically validating the technology integration model (TIM). Design/methodology/approach A self-administered online survey questionnaire was used to collect data among consumers who have experienced using SWDs in Malaysia. A total of 309 responses were considered valid for further analysis. SmartPLS 4-SEM (partial least squares) was employed to test the hypotheses. Findings The findings indicate that technological factors (i.e. healthology, perceived aesthetics) and agency feature (i.e., usability) are critical in explaining perceived usefulness and subsequently lead to confirmation. Perceived usefulness and perceived enjoyment have a significant positive effect on confirmation, while social influence has a significant positive effect on enjoyment and consumer brand identification. The findings also reveal that habit and confirmation have a significant positive direct effect on continuance intention to use SWDs. Practical implications This study provides actionable insights for developing SWDs strategies by emphasising technological features attributes and human psychological factors that motivate consumers to increase the likelihood of continuance intention to use rather than abandon it after a short period of usage. Social implications This study has important social implications for promoting sustained engagement with smart wearable devices (SWDs) as tools for preventive healthcare and healthier lifestyles. By combining health-related functionality, usability and aesthetically appealing design with enjoyment and habit-forming features, SWDs can encourage individuals to regularly monitor physical activity and other health indicators, potentially improving health awareness and supporting early behavioural intervention through improved self-management of well­being. Originality/value This study offers a novel theoretical understanding of TIM by integrating both technological features, confirmation and psychological factors into a single model. TIM explains the relationship between individuals and technology, emphasising parsimony and practicality in daily life.

title: When promises matter more than fairness: The dominant role of the psychological contract in driving organisational citizenship behaviour in a selected South African higher education institution
abstract: Orientation: South African universities increasingly rely on the discretionary efforts of academic staff to maintain high teaching and learning standards, research and innovation and community engagement. Perceived organisational justice has long been related to positive extra-role behaviours, while the role of the psychological contract, which is employees’ beliefs about mutual obligations with their employer, has received less attention as a dominant driver of organisational citizenship behaviour (OCB). Research purpose: The purpose was to test whether the psychological contract predicts OCB more strongly than organisational justice. Motivation for the study: Previous research emphasised organisational justice as a key driver of OCB. However, evidence suggests that fulfilled psychological contracts may matter more, especially in universities where resource constraints challenge fair treatment. Research approach/design and method: A quantitative cross-sectional survey design was applied, and data were collected from 340 academic staff using a structured questionnaire. Data were analysed using the PROCESS macro to test direct effects. Main findings: The results showed that organisational justice did not significantly predict OCB when the psychological contract was considered. The psychological contract emerged as a strong direct predictor of OCB, explaining a significant portion of its variance. Practical/managerial implications: Managers in higher education institution should prioritise fulfilling the psychological contract through clear communication and delivery on promises to promote OCB, rather than relying solely on perceived organisational justice. Contribution/value-add: This study extends the understanding of OCB antecedents by highlighting the dominant role of the psychological contract over organisational justice in a South African university context.

title: Unleashing Creative Entrepreneurial Mindsets in the Creative Economy for Career Intentions and HR Development in Creative SMEs for Achieving SDGs
journal: Journal of Business Management and Economic Development
abstract: The creative economy has become a key driver of economic growth, employment, and innovation. However, creative small and medium enterprises (SMEs) continue to face challenges in fostering a creative entrepreneurial mindset that supports sustainable career development. This study examines the effect of the creative entrepreneurial mindset on career intentions. It investigates how strategic human resource development (HRD), digitalization, access to technology, and social collaboration strengthen this relationship. The study employed a convergent mixed-methods design, integrating quantitative and qualitative approaches. The study analyzed quantitative data using Structural Equation Modelling (SEM-PLS) and examined qualitative data through thematic analysis in NVivo. The findings indicate that a creative entrepreneurial mindset significantly and positively influences career intentions. Strategic HRD practices focused on continuous learning and innovation enhance entrepreneurial capabilities, while digitalization and access to technology strengthen entrepreneurial opportunities. Social collaboration further reinforces sustainable career development through knowledge sharing and network support. This study contributes to the entrepreneurship and strategic HRD literature by proposing an integrated framework linking entrepreneurial mindset, organizational capability development, and digital transformation. The findings also support Sustainable Development Goals (SDG) 8 and SDG 9 by highlighting the importance of entrepreneurial capability development and digital innovation in promoting sustainable careers within creative SMEs.
authors: I Gede Eko Putra Sri Sentanu

title: Training-to-application gaps in digital agricultural practices: Exploratory evidence from agricultural actors in China
journal: Journal of Smart Farming and Food Security
abstract: Digital-skills training is increasingly used to advance agricultural digitalisation; however, participation and learning do not necessarily translate into application within production and business routines. This exploratory study investigates the training-to-application gap using 156 questionnaire records from agricultural actors in China recruited via convenience sampling through WeChat-based networks. The outcome is a broad, self-reported, four-category indicator of post-training digital application based on retrospective assessments of training experiences over the preceding two years, rather than a technology-specific measure of adoption, sustained use, or performance. Grounded in training-transfer theory, the analysis examines whether perceived content relevance, an inverse scenario/practice-barrier index, and course-linked post-training support are associated with higher reported application. Cumulative-logit estimates yielded no statistically detectable associations for the three indicators in the baseline model (likelihood-ratio test p = .995; McFadden pseudo-R² = .001). The conclusions concerning H1–H3 remained unchanged across alternative predictor coding, separate modelling of the two barrier components, and expanded covariate adjustment. An exploratory secondary finding indicated higher reported application among production-oriented respondents than among market- or service-oriented respondents; however, the broad outcome may not be fully comparable across business contexts. The study's principal contribution lies in conceptually distinguishing training participation, learning, initial trial, continued use, routinisation, and operational value. On this basis, the article advances a literature-informed Conditional Conversion Framework for future testing, in which technical feasibility, economic viability, platform and market fit, and ecosystem implementation support may enable or constrain progression across application stages.

title: The four-day working week: from managerial innovation to European policy experimentation
journal: International Journal of Sociology and Social Policy
abstract: Purpose This article maps the four-day working week (4DWW) as a policy idea in Europe. It contributes a theoretical map of working-time perspectives, a conceptual genealogy of the 4DWW from a compressed model to a reduced-hours formulation and a comparative mapping of recent European public policy initiatives, alongside working definitions of the concept and its policy expressions. Design/methodology/approach The study combines a theoretically guided conceptual-historical review of the academic and policy literature with a comparative mapping of European 4DWW public policy initiatives, identified through three criteria: European jurisdiction, public-authority involvement and legal enactment between January 2018 and January 2024. It draws on sources from the 1940s to 2026. Findings The analysis identifies three developments. First, the 4DWW has shifted from a compressed working week associated with managerial interests to a reduced working week engaging broader economic, social and environmental concerns; this entails a recombination of managerial and social-transformative framings. Second, recent years have seen unconventional labour public policies experimenting with a 4DWW, differing in their conceptual approach, sectoral scope, financial incentives and legal pathways. Third, this malleability complicates treatment of the 4DWW as an object of academic research. Originality/value This article complements recent systematic and scoping reviews of the workplace 4DWW literature by approaching the proposition through a theoretically grounded lens from the political economy of work, by proposing working definitions that clarify its persistent ambiguity and by analysing its emergence as a public policy across Europe. It offers a conceptual baseline for further comparative research and policy evaluation.

title: The eye as a canary in the coal mine: oculomics for psychiatry
The Impurity That Was Not: A Persistent Efinaconazole Signal Revealed as an Isotopologue
abstract: Abstract Identification of process-related impurities is a routine task in the optimization and manufacturing of APIs. The identification of these contaminants enables researchers to develop appropriate strategies to purge them or prevent their formation. In many cases, impurity identification is straightforward, relying on an understanding of the synthetic process and the reactivity of the reagents, which allows researchers to hypothesize the formation of specific byproducts that are often indeed generated during synthesis. In other instances, however, certain impurities are extremely difficult to characterize, and their identification becomes a challenging and demanding task, particularly when present at very low levels. This article describes the time- and resource-intensive effort required to identify and characterize a nonpurging impurity in efinaconazole that elutes in close proximity to the API peak and is consistently detected at 0.06% (a/a), posing a potential Out of Specification risk during industrial production. The impurity was ultimately identified as an isotopologue of efinaconazole exhibiting subtly distinct physicochemical properties, an uncommon behavior for isotopologue species.

title: The Falsity of Positive Technology Shocks
abstract: In mainstream macroeconomic models, random shocks drive economic outcomes. Macroeconomic shocks are typically categorized as positive or negative. However, all shocks are exogenous. Although many types of shocks exist, this article argues that there can be no such thing as a positive technological shock. Research and development are not exogenous. R&D requires savings, entrepreneurial insight, and risk-taking. Even an accidental discovery assumes that someone was using resources while looking for something. Because technological “shocks” require the application of research and development resources, they are not shocks. Thus, there is a flaw in how mainstream models represent growth. This article proposes that a proper theory of economic growth is founded on endogenous microeconomic theory.
